source.title: SMART: Scalable Multi-agent Real-time Simulation via Next-token Prediction
source.authors: Wei Wu; Xiaoxin Feng; Zi-Yan Gao; Yuheng Kan

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether a parameter-count power law for held-out cross-entropy loss applies in autonomous-driving motion generation, a non-text domain.
record.gate_note: The study reports a test-loss scaling fit for SMART models of different sizes. It also reports motion-generation metrics by model size, but those are not held-out cross-entropy losses or tests of a power-law fit. Scaling-law statements attributed to prior work are not study results.
record.test_reason: The study trains decoder-only next-token models (SMART) on discretised driving-motion tokens at four sizes (1.0M–101M). It fits a power law of held-out cross-entropy loss against parameter count (Sec. 4.3, Eq. 6, Fig. 4). That is a new-domain test of whether the power-law form holds beyond text (V5).
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that SMART shows scalability, with a power-law decrease in test loss as model size grows, plus zero-shot generalisation across datasets. They also claim insights into dataset-size scaling, but no data-scaling experiment is reported.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a parameter-size sweep and held-out cross-entropy loss, but applies them to driving-motion models rather than language models and reports a limited four-size range.

fits_no_version.finding: Sim Agents realism metrics rise steadily with model size from 1M to 101M (Table 9). Interactive goes 0.782 to 0.819 and map-based 0.835 to 0.872, while kinematic changes little (0.423 to 0.457). No predictive fit is given, and the models are not language models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Downstream task metrics of non-text next-token models improve monotonically with parameter count.

record.peer_reviewed: 38th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2024)
record.problems: The authors state that dataset size limited validation to models with a maximum scale of 100 million parameters. The scaling experiment covers four model sizes, and no uncertainty estimates are reported for the fit.
record.rows_left_out: No additional held-out cross-entropy scaling results are stated separately. Table 9 reports motion-generation metrics by model size, not cross-entropy loss or a power-law fit.

untested.parts: Only driving-motion token models with parameter-count scaling are tested. There is no data-size or compute scaling, although Eq. 5 names training tokens T and the text claims insight into dataset-size scaling. Image/video, repeated data, fine-tuning and transfer regimes are not tested.
No extrapolation from small fits to larger runs.
Depth and width co-vary with size; there is no fixed-N shape comparison.
No predictive fit of downstream metrics against scale or loss, and not language models.
No comparison of fitting choices or setups.

missing.what: Per-size downstream Sim Agents metrics (kinematic, interactive, map-based) for SMART 1M/7M/26M/101M, showing monotone gains with scale. A researcher comparing downstream scaling in non-text domains would need these.

record.verdict_notes: Not an original source. Only parameter scaling is measured. The training data includes a proprietary dataset (0.68B of the 1B tokens), which limits reproducibility. The authors state that dataset size capped validation at about 100M parameters.

versions.untested_parts: The models are autonomous-driving motion models, not language models.
No experiment is reported in which a fit from smaller runs predicts the loss of much larger runs.
No fixed-compute comparison or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation is reported.
The study does not isolate depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
Tests driving-motion generation only; does not test image/video models, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer as scaling regimes.
Does not test downstream-task performance as a predictable function of scale or pretraining loss.
Does not compare fitting methods or setups to test exponent or allocation sensitivity, or whether curves bend away from a power law.

rows.subject: SMART 1M, SMART 7M, SMART 26M, SMART 101M (scaling fit)
rows.size_stated: 1M to 101M parameters; Table 5 gives total parameters 1.0M, 7.2M, 26.9M, and 101.0M
rows.operation_detail: Measured validation test cross-entropy loss across model sizes and fitted a power law against parameter count.
rows.measure: Final test cross-entropy loss L, described as reducible loss normalized by irreducible loss
rows.value: log(L) = -0.157log(X) + 1.52; for the model-parameter scaling experiment, X is N
rows.note: The text describes a clear power-law trend across the tested SMART model sizes. Figure 4 also plots loss curves, but no per-model loss values are stated in the text.
rows.check: Link and state are correct. Caveats for the record: the fit covers only four sizes over about two orders of magnitude. Data is fixed at 1B tokens, so larger models may be data-limited. No goodness-of-fit or per-model loss values are given. How the 'irreducible loss' normalisation was estimated is not stated. Table 5 shows the motion-token vocabulary changing across sizes (512, 1024, 1024, 2048), which makes cross-entropy values not strictly comparable. The text also mislabels α as the exponent; the slope is β = −0.157.

relationships.condition: SMART driving-motion next-token models, 1M–101M parameters, fixed 1B-token training set, WOMD validation loss
relationships.reason: Authors report a clear power-law fit, log(L) = −0.157 log(N) + 1.52, across the four sizes (R1). The evidence is thin: four points, no fit uncertainty, and vocabulary size changes across models.
relationships.display_finding: Validation loss fitted log(L)=−0.157 log(N)+1.52 across four sizes, without fit uncertainty and with vocabulary size changing across models.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
